name: Lacy's Caves
text: Your train passes near Lacy's Caves, on the train's {side}, five chambers carved into the red sandstone cliff of the River Eden in the 18th century for Lieutenant-Colonel Samuel Lacy of nearby Salkeld Hall. No one knows why they were made, but Lacy used them to entertain his guests, among ornamental gardens.

name: Acorn Bank Garden & Watermill
text: Your train passes near Acorn Bank, on the train's {side}, a National Trust garden sheltered by old oaks and high walls, growing more than 250 medicinal and culinary herbs. The estate has a partly restored watermill that works, powered by Crowdundle Beck.

name: Smardale Viaduct
text: Your train crosses Smardale Viaduct, about 40 metres high and the highest on the Settle to Carlisle line. Built of local limestone, it took five years to build, opening in 1875, and it spans both Scandal Beck and the trackbed of the old Stainmore railway.

name: Dandry Mire Viaduct
text: Your train crosses Dandry Mire Viaduct, about 15 metres high and 210 metres long. The builders planned an embankment across the bog here, but Dandry Mire swallowed everything that was tipped into it, so they built a viaduct instead.

name: Rise Hill Tunnel
text: Your train goes through Rise Hill Tunnel, more than a kilometre long under Black Moss. It is the second longest tunnel on the Settle to Carlisle line, after Blea Moor, and work on it began in May 1870.

name: Ribblehead Viaduct
text: Your train crosses Ribblehead Viaduct, the longest structure on the Settle to Carlisle line, with 24 arches across Batty Moss. Up to 2,300 men worked on it, most living in shanty towns near its foot, and the last stone was laid in 1874.

name: Corby Bridge
text: Your train crosses Corby Bridge, also called Wetheral Viaduct, five great arches faced in red sandstone, about 33 metres above the River Eden. Built from 1830 to 1834 for the Newcastle and Carlisle Railway, one of the earliest main lines, it is listed at Grade I.

name: Thirlwall Castle
text: Your train passes near Thirlwall Castle, on the train's {side}, a 12th-century castle on the bank of the River Tipalt. It was strengthened with stones taken from Hadrian's Wall nearby, and began to fall into ruin in the 17th century.

name: Kendal Castle
text: Your train passes near the ruins of Kendal Castle, on the train's {side}, on top of a glacial drumlin above the town. It was the seat of the Barons of Kendal, and by the 15th century it belonged to the Parr family, ancestors of Catherine Parr, the sixth wife of Henry VIII.

name: The Castle Dairy
text: Your train passes near the Castle Dairy, on the train's {side}, a medieval house that may be the oldest building in the town to have been lived in without a break. Listed at Grade I, it keeps carvings, fireplaces and original windows, and is now a restaurant.

name: St Margaret's Tower
text: Your train passes near St Margaret's Tower, on the train's {side}, the oldest building in the village and all that is left of a medieval church. It is kept as a clock tower, with a plaque to local men who served in South Africa in 1900 to 1901.

name: School Knott
text: Your train passes near School Knott, on the train's {side}, a hill with a chapter of its own in Wainwright's The Outlying Fells of Lakeland. His walk up it starts at the railway station, and from the top four separate stretches of the lake can be seen.

name: Liverpool Town Hall
text: Your train passes under the streets near Liverpool Town Hall, on the train's {side}, built from 1749 to 1754 to a design by John Wood the Elder. After a fire in 1795 it was largely rebuilt, with a dome by James Wyatt, and its listing calls it one of the finest surviving 18th-century town halls.

name: Bluecoat Chambers
text: Your train passes under the streets near Bluecoat Chambers, on the train's {side}, built in 1716 to 1717 as a charity school and the oldest surviving building in central Liverpool. It is now the Bluecoat, which claims to be the oldest arts centre in Britain.

name: The Cavern Club
text: Your train passes beneath the streets just by the Cavern Club, on the train's {side}, which opened as a jazz club in 1957 and became closely linked with Merseybeat, with the Beatles playing there often in their early years. It closed in 1973 and was filled in while Merseyrail's underground lines were being built, reopening in 1984.

name: St George's Hall, Liverpool
text: Your train passes under the streets near St George's Hall, on the train's {side}, a Neoclassical building of 1854 holding concert halls and law courts. The architectural historian Nikolaus Pevsner called it one of the finest neo-Grecian buildings in the world.

name: St Johns Beacon
text: Your train passes under the streets near St Johns Beacon, on the train's {side}, a tower 138 metres tall, built in 1969 and opened by Queen Elizabeth II. It had a revolving restaurant at the top, reached by lifts in 30 seconds or by 558 stairs.

name: Carlisle Bridge, Lancaster
text: Your train crosses the River Lune on Carlisle Bridge, first built in the 1840s for the Lancaster and Carlisle Railway. Its spans were laminated timber at first, then iron from 1866 and steel and concrete from 1963, but the original piers are still in place.

name: Salford Lads' Club
text: Your train passes near Salford Lads' Club, on the train's {side}, built for boys in 1903 and opened in January 1904 by Robert Baden-Powell, who later founded the Scouts. Its former members include Graham Nash of the Hollies, and its tiled interior and boxing ring are largely unchanged.

name: River Irwell Railway Bridge
text: Your train passes near the River Irwell Railway Bridge, on the train's {side}, built in stone by George Stephenson in 1830 to carry the Liverpool and Manchester Railway into its terminus at Liverpool Road. It is listed at Grade I.

name: Mamucium
text: Your train passes near the site of Mamucium, on the train's {side}, a Roman fort also known as Mancunium. Most of it was levelled during the Industrial Revolution, but part of its wall and its gatehouse have been rebuilt and are open to the public.

name: Salford Cathedral
text: Your train passes near Salford Cathedral, on the train's {side}, built from 1844 to 1848 as the first cruciform Catholic church in England since the Reformation. Its front and nave are smaller copies of those at Howden Minster, and its choir is modelled on Selby Abbey's.

name: Norcliffe Chapel
text: Your train passes near Norcliffe Chapel, on the train's {side}, built in 1822 to 1823 by Samuel Greg, founder of Quarry Bank Mill, for his workers. The National Trust has owned it since 1977, but it is still a working Unitarian chapel.

name: Church of St Benedict, Ardwick
text: Your train passes near the Church of St Benedict, on the train's {side}, built in 1880 and thought to be the architect J. S. Crowther's masterpiece. It is no longer used for worship, and housed a climbing centre until July 2025.

name: Mayfield Park, Manchester
text: Your train passes near Mayfield Park, on the train's {side}, opened in September 2022 as the city centre's first new park in more than 100 years. It takes its name from Mayfield, a former railway station close by.

name: Unthank Hall
text: Your train passes near Unthank Hall, on the train's {side}, a 16th-century house on the bank of the South Tyne that takes in an older pele tower. It was rebuilt in neo-Tudor style from 1862 to 1865 by the Newcastle architect John Dobson.

name: Beltingham River Shingle
text: Your train passes near Beltingham River Shingle, on the train's {side}, a Site of Special Scientific Interest on the South Tyne. High levels of heavy metals from the North Pennine orefield, which the river drains, have built up in its shingle, and an unusual community of plants that tolerate them grows there.

name: Constantius Bridge
text: Your train passes near Constantius Bridge, on the train's {side}, which carries the A69 over the Tyne just downstream of the Meeting of the Waters, where the North and South Tyne join. It is the last bridge over the Tyne before the river splits in two.

name: Dilston Castle
text: Your train passes near Dilston Castle, on the train's {side}, a ruined three-storey tower house built in the 15th century by Sir William Claxton. In the 17th century it passed to the Radclyffe family, later the Earls of Derwentwater.

name: Corbridge Bridge
text: Your train passes near a 17th-century stone bridge of seven arches over the Tyne, on the train's {side}, on a crossing used since a bridge was first built here in 1235. It was the only bridge on the Tyne to survive the Great Flood of 1771.

name: St Andrew's Church, Bywell
text: Your train passes near St Andrew's Church, Bywell, on the train's {side}, whose massive tower was built for defence in about 850. The church is no longer used for regular worship and is cared for by the Churches Conservation Trust.

name: Cherryburn
text: Your train passes near Cherryburn, on the train's {side}, the cottage where the wood engraver and ornithologist Thomas Bewick was born in 1753. The National Trust runs it as a museum, with a large collection of his books and engravings.

name: Ovingham Bridge
text: Your train passes near Ovingham Bridge, on the train's {side}, a toll bridge of 1883 that replaced a ferry over the Tyne. Its steel tubes are marked Dorman Long Middlesbrough, the firm that designed and built the Sydney Harbour Bridge and the Tyne Bridge.

name: George Stephenson's Birthplace
text: Your train passes near the cottage where the railway pioneer George Stephenson was born in 1781, on the train's {side}, across the Tyne. The stone cottage was built in about 1750 and now belongs to the National Trust.

name: River Derwent, North East England
text: Your train crosses the River Derwent near where it joins the Tyne at Derwenthaugh. Its name comes from Brythonic words for oak and valley, and it flows for 35 miles, passing through the Derwent Reservoir west of Consett.

name: Derwent Tower
text: Your train passes near the site of Derwent Tower, on the train's {side}, a 29-storey block of flats opened in 1972. Its unusual shape earned it the nickname the Dunston Rocket while it was being built, and it was demolished in 2012.

name: King Edward VII Bridge
text: Your train crosses the Tyne on the King Edward VII Bridge, opened by the King and Queen Alexandra in July 1906 and called Britain's last great railway bridge. Before it was built, trains through the city had to reverse out of the station.

name: Chester Burn Viaduct
text: Your train crosses Chester Burn Viaduct, which towers over the marketplace at the north end of the town. It was finished in 1868 for the new line through the Team Valley, and now carries the East Coast Main Line.
